Installation

Source: vignettes/Installation.Rmd
Installation.Rmd

Before you start

RiboPilot runs its analysis inside a container: Docker on a workstation, or Singularity (also called Apptainer) on a computing cluster. The container holds every analysis tool, so you do not install them yourself.

RiboPilot is developed and tested on Linux. On a Mac it needs Docker Desktop. On Windows, use WSL2 and run R inside WSL. On a cluster, use Singularity or Apptainer (see Running on a cluster).

Disk space. The container image is about 2.6 GB to download and 7.7 GB on disk. Each project also needs room for its own files: the test project used 1.6 GB, mostly Nextflow’s working files (0.9 GB) and the taxonomy copy (0.5 GB). Reference databases are small: the two built for the test project took 4 MB and 16 MB. Disk space, caches, and offline use says where each of these goes, and how to move it.

Install the tools

Install each of these once, and check it with the command beside it.

  1. Docker (workstation). On Linux, add yourself to the docker group so Docker runs without sudo. On a Mac, start Docker Desktop. Check: docker run hello-world. On a cluster, use Singularity or Apptainer instead. Check: singularity --version.

  2. Java 17 or newer. Check: java -version.

  3. Nextflow, a version from 24.10 through 25.10. Check: nextflow -v. If you have a newer Nextflow, RiboPilot runs version 25.10.6 instead. To set this yourself, add export NXF_VER=25.10.6 to your shell profile.

  4. R 4.4.0 or newer. Check: R --version.

  5. RiboPilot, in R:

    install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("NMNH-OceanDNA/RiboPilot")

You do not need to download the RiboPilot container image. This will happen automatically the first time you run the pipeline.

Check that it works

Run the test project: see Get started.

Optional: an NCBI API key

An NCBI API key lets RiboPilot query NCBI faster. It is free to set up. The simplest place for it is your ~/.Renviron file, next to any other keys:

NCBI_API_KEY=<your key>

Restart R after you edit the file. RiboPilot then passes the key to every run and every reference build, without writing it into the project’s .config file.

Alternatively, you can pass the key to RiboPilot::new_project() as ncbi_api_key; it is then stored in the project’s .config file and shows in the Nextflow command of the run window.

Never paste your key into a screenshot, an email, or a GitHub issue.

Upgrading RiboPilot

Run these in R, one step at a time:

# 1. Remove the installed RiboPilot
remove.packages("RiboPilot")

# 2. Restart R
#    RStudio: Session > Restart R, or run rstudioapi::restartSession()
#    Elsewhere: quit R and start it again

# 3. Install the new version
remotes::install_github("NMNH-OceanDNA/RiboPilot")

# 4. Update existing projects as needed, once per project
RiboPilot::backwards_compatibility("~/my_project")

The changelog lists what changed.

The backwards_compatibility function brings the project’s database up to date and points the project at the container image for the RiboPilot version you installed. The next run downloads that image by itself, so there is nothing to pull by hand. Your samples, results, and settings are kept. Before it changes anything, RiboPilot saves a copy of the database (.sqlite.bak.<timestamp>) and of the project’s .config (.config.bak.<timestamp>) in the project folder. To see what would change without changing anything, add dry_run = TRUE.

What you see if you skip backwards_compatibility:

  • The database is out of date. The app does not open, and says “This project needs an update. Run backwards_compatibility(…) first.”
  • Only the container image is out of date. The app opens and says “Container version does not match RiboPilot”. Runs may still work, but with the code and tools in the older image.

Each image takes about 7.7 GB in Docker, or about 2.5 GB as a Singularity file. Once no project uses an old one image, remove it with docker image rm <image>; with Singularity, delete its file from your image cache (see Disk space, caches, and offline use).
